records.quote: there sat a woman in long, black clothes; and she said, "Death has been in thy chamber, and I saw him hasten away with thy little child
records.paraphrase: A personified figure called Night appears and reports seeing Death.

records.quote: I am Night; I saw thy tears whilst thou sang'st them!
records.paraphrase: The woman in black identifies herself as Night, a personified entity.

records.quote: every person has his or her life's tree or flower, just as everyone happens to be settled; they look like other plants, but they have pulsations of the heart.
records.paraphrase: An explanation that each person's life corresponds to a plant with a beating heart.

records.quote: the distressed mother bent down over all the smallest plants, and heard within them how the human heart beat; and amongst millions she knew her child's.
records.paraphrase: The mother searches among the plants, listening for heartbeats to identify her child.

records.quote: She was so downcast, so afraid that it should die!
records.paraphrase: The mother is deeply distressed and fearful her sick child will die.

records.quote: Then she lay down to drink up the lake, and that was an impossibility for a human being, but the afflicted mother thought that a miracle might happen nevertheless.
records.paraphrase: The mother attempts an impossible act, hoping for a miracle.

records.quote: I am His gardener, I take all His flowers and trees, and plant them out in the great garden of Paradise, in the unknown land
records.paraphrase: Death explains his role as a gardener transplanting human-lives to Paradise.

records.quote: the thornbush shot forth fresh green leaves, and there came flowers on it in the cold winter night, the heart of the afflicted mother was so warm
records.paraphrase: The thorn-bush miraculously blooms when warmed by the mother's heart.

records.quote: Then the mother screamed with terror, "Which of them was my child? Tell it me! Save the innocent! Save my child from all that misery!
records.paraphrase: The mother reacts with terror upon learning one future is her child's fate.

records.quote: "Yes," said the thorn-bush; "but I will not tell thee which way he took, unless thou wilt first warm me up at thy heart.
records.paraphrase: A thorn-bush speaks and bargains with the mother.

records.quote: "Oh, hear me not when I pray against Thy will, which is the best! hear me not! hear me not!"
records.paraphrase: The mother relents and prays for God's will to be done.

records.quote: her eyes sunk down in the depths of the waters, and became two precious pearls; but the water bore her up, as if she sat in a swing
records.paraphrase: The mother's eyes turn into pearls and the water carries her across.

criteria.rationale: The plant-heartbeat and gardener conceits are allegorical/supernatural, not scientific facts, theories, or speculative sciences. No material scientific content is represented.
No device, technique, or engineered invention affects the setting or outcome. The clock and greenhouse are ordinary or magical props, not inventions materially driving the story.
The setting is a folkloric present with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement. The vision of a child's future in the well is prophecy/allegory, not time travel.
The story is a moral/religious allegory; it does not extrapolate consequences from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise.

The mother listening for her child's heartbeat among plants is intuitive maternal recognition within a magical framework, not observation, hypothesis, testing, or systematic evidential inference driving understanding.

A strange mile-broad house across a lake and Death's greenhouse leading to the 'unknown land' of Paradise are nonordinary otherworldly environments, and Night and Death function as visitors. However these are religious/allegorical realms rather than cosmic or dimensional environments in the SF sense, so materiality and interpretation are uncertain.

The central event is a single child's death and the mother's grief\u2014a personal misfortune without large-scale disaster. No natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused catastrophe of broad scale is present.

candidates.description: A cosmology in which every human life corresponds to a living plant or tree in Death's vast greenhouse, each with a beating heart, tended and transplanted by Death acting as God's gardener who relocates lives to Paradise.

novelty.rationale: The correspondence of each human life to a plant in Death's greenhouse, complete with audible heartbeats and Death's role as a transplanting gardener, is a totalizing reconception of mortality and the cosmos that departs radically from the empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: While the plant-life system has an internal consistency, the story's logic is explicitly supernatural and theological: personified Night and Death, a bargaining thorn-bush, eyes transmuting into pearls, and Death acting on 'OUR LORD's bidding'. These are magical/religious rather than a systematic, immanent, nonsupernatural account. The framework is allegorical fairy-tale, not imaginary science or social organization.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The greenhouse cosmology and Death's gardener role govern the climax: the mother's search by heartbeat, her confrontation with Death over the crocus, and the resolution of the whole narrative hinge on this system.

estrangement.rationale: The reader encounters an estranging inversion of ordinary botany and death: plants that are human lives with beating hearts, tended in a cosmic greenhouse, contrasting sharply with the empirical world of the sick child's bedside.

candidates.description: Death and Night personified as literal agents who move through the world, converse, bargain, and take children away.

novelty.rationale: The literal personification of abstract forces as acting characters differs totally from the empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: These personifications are supernatural allegorical figures operating under a theological/religious logic ('I only do His bidding'), with no systematic, immanent, nonsupernatural account. This is fairy-tale magic, failing cognitive validation.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: Death and Night as agents drive the entire plot of pursuit and confrontation.

estrangement.rationale: Abstract forces made flesh estrange the reader from the ordinary experience of death and night as impersonal phenomena.

candidates.description: A world where a thorn-bush speaks and blooms when warmed at a heart, and a mother's eyes become pearls allowing water to bear her across a lake.

novelty.rationale: Talking plants and bodily transmutation into pearls constitute world-altering departures from the empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: These are explicitly miraculous events (the text names them 'a miracle'), with no systematic or nonsupernatural mechanism. They fail cognitive validation as magical fairy-tale motifs.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: These transformations are episodic trials along the mother's journey rather than governing the overriding narrative logic, which is set by Death and the greenhouse cosmology.

estrangement.rationale: Sacrificial bargains yielding blooming thorns and pearl-eyes estrange the reader from ordinary cause and effect.
